name: Ear
baseMeaning: A picture of a single human ear in side profile, the inner folds curved inward. Read in a message it lands as listening, hearing something, or paying attention.
tldr: 👂 Ear. In a chat it comes across as listening, hearing something, or paying attention.

contextMeanings.meaning: The plain reading: a single human ear in side profile, the inner folds curved inward. Nothing hidden in the drawing itself.
contextMeanings.example: Telling a friend you are on a call listening 👂

contextMeanings.meaning: Borrowed as a reaction, it reads as listening, hearing something, or paying attention.
contextMeanings.example: Reacting when someone says something surprising 👂

contextMeanings.meaning: In a dating thread the gesture is usually doing the work of a line that was not typed. It arrives as listening, hearing something, or paying attention, softened by whatever sentence sits next to it.

In a work channel it is read the same way it is read anywhere else — listening, hearing something, or paying attention — but the stakes of a misread are higher, because the sender is often talking about somebody's actual work.

platformNotes.note: In Slack 👂 lands in channels where the sentence was supposed to be shorter. It is usually standing in for telling a friend you are on a call listening, and a channel where the topic is somebody's workload is where it misreads.
On Discord 👂 is a staple of the reaction bar, which is why it so often arrives stripped of its listening, hearing something, or paying attention reading — a shape pressed rather than a message sent.

On X and Twitter 👂 does most of its work in replies, where it tags a message like reacting when someone says something surprising. Short enough to survive being the whole post, which is exactly why it is used that way.

On iOS the Ear 👂 renders as the neutral drawing, and the neutral swatch is what most people send without thinking about it. A message like telling a friend you are on a call listening is the kind that carries it — the picture lands before the sentence does.

WhatsApp renders 👂 exactly as the phone system does, but the keyboard keeps it in the body-parts section, where nobody looks unless they are hunting for it. In family threads it tends to accompany a message like reacting when someone says something surprising.

generationalNotes.note: Gen Z reaches for 👂 to do the work of telling a friend you are on a call listening, and treats the neutral drawing as the default rather than as a choice. What they hear first is listening, hearing something, or paying attention.

Millennials tend to send 👂 deliberately, usually for something like reacting when someone says something surprising, and they read listening, hearing something, or paying attention into it more often than the older cohorts do.
Gen X mostly uses 👂 literally, as the picture of the gesture itself, and is less likely to read listening, hearing something, or paying attention into it than younger senders are.
Older senders use 👂 in the most straightforward way, on family and group messages, and are less likely to hear the listening, hearing something, or paying attention subtext in it.

warnings.title: 👂 and 🦻 get swapped
warnings.description: The Ear with Hearing Aid 🦻 is one tap away in every picker, and it does not carry the same reading — the hearing aid version adds the device behind the ear and gets used when hearing itself is the subject. Check which one you actually picked.

warnings.title: The reading it usually gets is not the one it was sent with
warnings.description: People take 👂 as something else fairly often: it gets taken as "sounds good" when it usually means "I am listening to you right now", because the ear alone signals attention rather than agreement. The sentence around it is usually what settles the meaning.

seoTitle: 👂 Ear Emoji - What It Actually Means in Text
seoDescription: 👂 Ear meaning: listening, hearing something, or paying attention. How the emoji is used at work, at home and in dating threads, and where it goes wrong.

longForm.overview:
The drawing of 👂 is a single human ear in side profile, the inner folds curved inward. It arrived with Unicode 6.0 in the body-parts section, and in a conversation it does the work of a line somebody left out on purpose.

The line it stands in for is listening, hearing something, or paying attention. That is the reading most people arrive with, and it is usually the intended one — a picture carries the same meaning as the sentence it replaces, and it arrives first.

The complication is that the drawing invites a second reading. It gets taken as "sounds good" when it usually means "I am listening to you right now", because the ear alone signals attention rather than agreement. In practice that second reading is not rare — it is the one that decides how a message lands, because the sender has usually not thought about it at all.

It also sits in the crowded part of the picker. The nearest neighbour is 🦻 Ear with Hearing Aid: the hearing aid version adds the device behind the ear and gets used when hearing itself is the subject. The two are close enough that a fast thumb picks the wrong one, and the message goes out carrying a meaning nobody chose.

The ear also exists in five skin tones. They are separate pages with separate copy, because picking a tone is a decision in a way that picking the plain emoji is not: it says something about who the sender thinks the reader is.

In short — the ear reads as listening, hearing something, or paying attention, it is most often used for telling a friend you are on a call listening or reacting when someone says something surprising, and the five tone pages under it each say something different about who is sending it. The rest of the page takes those three apart.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
Context, not the picture, decides how this lands. 👂 in a work thread is reacting when someone says something surprising; 👂 in a family thread is telling a friend you are on a call listening; 👂 in a thread with somebody you like is a way of saying something you would rather not type out.

The tone versions of the emoji make the same point from the other side. The gesture is identical in all five, and the swatch says something about the sender before a word is read.

The shortest messages are the risky ones. A lone 👂 is the whole reply, and it is carrying a meaning nobody wrote down — listening, hearing something, or paying attention is the intention, but what arrives is a drawing. Everything the sentence would have disambiguated is simply missing.

Put it this way. Telling a friend you are on a call listening is the job the ear does most: it saves a sentence and lands faster than one would have. Reacting when someone says something surprising is the job it does second: there the picture is not the point, it is the temperature of the message.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
Think about what the emoji is replacing. If the sentence under it is doing the real work, 👂 will get taken as "sounds good" when it usually means "I am listening to you right now", because the ear alone signals attention rather than agreement instead, and the thread ends up carrying a meaning nobody wrote.

And keep it away from first contact. There is nothing warm in the drawing, and a ear gesture used to answer other people's messages tends to sound like it is settling a point.

Keep it out of the formal register. In a thread about somebody's work, or in a message to somebody you have not met, 👂 reads as listening, hearing something, or paying attention, and formality is exactly where that reading does the most damage.

Leave 🦻 Ear with Hearing Aid for the other message. The hearing aid version adds the device behind the ear and gets used when hearing itself is the subject. And keep 👂 out of threads where somebody is hurting: it reads as listening, hearing something, or paying attention there, because there is nothing in the drawing that says you meant well.
longForm.howToReply:
The safe move in an unclear thread is to answer the text. 👂 gets taken as "sounds good" when it usually means "I am listening to you right now", because the ear alone signals attention rather than agreement often enough that the sentence matters more than the picture.

And do not send 👂 alone when the message underneath is supposed to be warm. A message like telling a friend you are on a call listening carries the feeling; the picture on its own leaves the reader choosing between listening, hearing something, or paying attention and something sharper.

Start by reading what the 👂 was doing. If it was a reaction, react: 👂 back, and the thread is closed. If it was aimed at you, write. The difference matters, because the reply to a reaction can be a picture and the reply to a request cannot.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 👂 and its skin-tone versions?
faqs.answer: The tone variants under ear show the same gesture in five different skin tones. The gesture does not change, but the tone is a small signal about who the sender imagines the reader is, and in some groups that signal is read louder than the sentence.

faqs.question: What does 👂 mean in text?
faqs.answer: 👂 is used for listening, hearing something, or paying attention. The drawing shows a single human ear in side profile, the inner folds curved inward, and that part is not in dispute — what changes is whether the sender is being literal or borrowing the gesture for a reaction.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 👂 and 🦻?
faqs.answer: The hearing aid version adds the device behind the ear and gets used when hearing itself is the subject. The two sit close together in most pickers, so the difference is often about which one the sender pressed rather than about what they meant.

faqs.question: Is 👂 rude?
faqs.answer: It can be. The gesture is meant as listening, hearing something, or paying attention, but it gets taken as "sounds good" when it usually means "I am listening to you right now", because the ear alone signals attention rather than agreement. The risk is highest when it is the only message in the thread — a sentence gives the picture some context to sit in.

faqs.question: What does 👂 mean from a guy?
faqs.answer: Nothing gender-specific. The same reading applies whoever sends it, and the meaning is set by the thread and by what is written next to it rather than by the sender.

conversationExamples.interpretation: A public sign-off, with the emoji as the full stop. The picture is doing the punctuation, which is why it is sent instead of a sentence.

conversationExamples.message: telling a friend you are on a call listening 👂
conversationExamples.interpretation: The everyday use: the picture carries the whole line. It lands as listening, hearing something, or paying attention, and matching it with the same emoji is a normal reply.

conversationExamples.message: reacting when someone says something surprising 👂
conversationExamples.interpretation: A handover or a sign-off in a channel. It reads as listening, hearing something, or paying attention, and naming the next step in words is usually clearer than leaving it to the gesture.

conversationExamples.message: there is something you should know 👂
conversationExamples.interpretation: A small joke or a nudge, with the emoji doing the tone work. It gets taken as "sounds good" when it usually means "I am listening to you right now", because the ear alone signals attention rather than agreement more easily here than it does in a work thread, because the thread is thinner.

conversationExamples.message: telling a friend you are on a call listening 👂
conversationExamples.interpretation: Family threads are where this lands most naturally. The reading is listening, hearing something, or paying attention, and nobody in the thread is reading it as anything sharper than that.
